chapter.name: Journey Inside the Atom
chapter.blurb: Traces the atom from Acharya Kanada's parmanu and Dalton's indivisible particle through Thomson's plum-pudding model, Rutherford's gold-foil experiment and nuclear model, and Bohr's shell model, to the discovery of the proton and neutron; then builds up atomic number, mass number, electronic configuration and valency for the first 18 elements, and closes with isotopes, average atomic mass and isobars.

scope_in.item: Trace how the idea of an indivisible particle of matter developed, from Acharya Kanada's parmanu and the Greek atomos to John Dalton's 1808 atomic theory
Describe J. J. Thomson's discovery of the electron from his cathode ray tube experiment, and his plum pudding model of the atom
Describe the gold foil (alpha-particle scattering) experiment and state why its results could not be explained by Thomson's model
State Rutherford's nuclear/planetary model of the atom, its estimate of the relative size of the nucleus, and why it could not explain atomic stability
Describe Rutherford's discovery of the proton and the rule that a neutral atom's number of protons equals its number of electrons
State Bohr's model of the atom: fixed shells/energy levels named K, L, M, N (or n = 1, 2, 3, 4), and how an electron changes shells by absorbing or releasing energy
Describe James Chadwick's 1932 discovery of the neutron and why it was needed to explain an atom's mass
State the symbol and relative charge of the electron, proton and neutron (Table 8.1), and how the ratio of protons to neutrons changes from light to heavy elements
Explain how element symbols are formed, including the IUPAC capitalisation rule and symbols derived from Latin, Greek or German names (Table 8.2)
Define atomic number (Z) as the number of protons, equal to the number of electrons in a neutral atom
Define mass number (A) as protons plus neutrons, and write an atom in standard notation, e.g. mass number 12 / atomic number 6 for carbon

Apply the Bohr-Bury rules (2n^2 maximum per shell, 8 maximum in the outermost shell except a first shell's 2, and filling from K outward) to state the electronic configuration of any of the first 18 elements (Table 8.4)
Define valence shell, valence electrons and the octet rule, and state that an octet (or 2 electrons for a single shell) makes an atom stable
Determine an element's valency from its valence electron count (lose if fewer than 4, gain if more than 4, share if exactly 4) or from a compound's formula such as H2O, NH3 or MgCl2
Define isotopes as atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, using hydrogen's and carbon's isotopes as examples
Explain that isotopes have identical chemical properties (same valence electrons) but different physical properties
Name the uses of the isotopes given in the chapter: uranium-235 as reactor fuel, cobalt-60 in cancer radiotherapy, iodine-131 for thyroid/goitre treatment, and carbon-14 in dating fossils
Calculate the weighted average atomic mass of an element from the percentage abundance of its isotopes, as worked for chlorine and set as a problem for bromine
Define isobars as atoms of different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers, using calcium, potassium and argon

concepts.name: Origins of Atomic Theory: Ancient Ideas to Dalton
concepts.description: How the idea of an indivisible particle of matter developed from Acharya Kanada's parmanu and the Greek atomos to John Dalton's 1808 scientific atomic theory.
concepts.idea: Long before experiments could test it, thinkers in ancient India and Greece imagined that matter could only be divided so far before reaching an indivisible particle.
concepts.rule: Acharya Kanada called the smallest, imperceptible particle a parmanu, which combines into dyads and triads to build all matter; the Greek philosophers Leucippus and Democritus called it atomos (indivisible). Both ideas were philosophical, not experimental. In 1808, John Dalton proposed the first scientific atomic theory, based on experiments, stating that all matter is made of indivisible atoms that are the fundamental building blocks of matter.
concepts.example: A parmanu combining with another parmanu forms a dyad (a group of two); Dalton's theory was the scientific starting point for the atomic models that followed.

questions.q: Explain why the concept of the 'atom' is said to have originated as an imaginary idea rather than from experimental observation, giving one example.
questions.a: The earliest ideas of the atom (Kanada's parmanu, and Leucippus and Democritus's atomos) came from reasoning and philosophical thought, with no experiments to test them; for example, Kanada's description of parmanus combining into dyads and triads was not based on any measured experiment.

questions.q: List two of the questions scientists asked after Dalton proposed his atomic theory.
questions.a: Any two of: what are atoms made up of; what would atoms look like if we could see them; what makes the atoms of one element different from another element's atoms.

questions.q: Compare Acharya Kanada's parmanu, the Greek atomos, and Dalton's atomic theory in terms of who proposed each idea, its basis (reasoning vs experiment), and roughly how long before Dalton each idea appeared.
questions.a: Kanada's parmanu (ancient India) and the Greek atomos (Leucippus and Democritus) were both philosophical ideas proposed over 2,000 years before Dalton, based on reasoning alone; Dalton's atomic theory (1808) was proposed far more recently and was based on scientific experiments, making it the first scientific description of matter's structure.
s: Kanada and the Greeks: philosophical, over 2000 years earlier

questions.q: Consider: (I) Acharya Kanada's parmanu could not be perceived by the senses. (II) John Dalton's atomic theory was based on philosophical reasoning rather than experiments. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I
o: Only I
Only II
Both I and II
Neither I nor II

questions.q: A student claims Dalton was the first person in history to think matter has a smallest, indivisible particle. Is this claim correct? Explain.
questions.a: No. Acharya Kanada in ancient India and Leucippus and Democritus in ancient Greece proposed similar ideas (parmanu and atomos) more than 2,000 years before Dalton; what made Dalton's theory different was that it was based on scientific experiments, not that it was the first such idea.
s: Correct reasoning with the real distinction

questions.q: Explain why the fact that ancient Indian and Greek thinkers independently arrived at a similar idea of an indivisible particle is described in the chapter as 'remarkably parallel', and what this suggests about the question they were both asking.
questions.a: Two separate civilisations, with no contact recorded between them on this idea, both concluded that matter must eventually reach a smallest, indivisible particle when repeatedly divided; this is called remarkably parallel because they reached a similar fundamental answer to the same fundamental question -- 'what is everything made up of?' -- independently, through reasoning alone, showing this was a natural and compelling question for early thinkers everywhere.

questions.q: Do you agree that a philosophical idea with no experimental evidence, like Kanada's parmanu, still deserves a place in the history of atomic theory? Justify your answer.
questions.a: A reasoned answer either way is acceptable if justified; for example, yes, because it shows early thinkers asking the right fundamental question and arriving at a conceptually similar answer to modern atomic theory, even though it could not be tested at the time.

questions.q: Design a short timeline (with at least four points) showing how the idea of the atom changed from Acharya Kanada to Dalton's atomic theory, including roughly how the basis of each idea (reasoning vs experiment) changed.
questions.a: Example timeline: (1) Acharya Kanada (ancient India) -- parmanu, indivisible, reasoning-based; (2) Leucippus and Democritus (ancient Greece) -- atomos, indivisible, reasoning-based, roughly parallel to Kanada; (3) many centuries pass with no major change to the idea; (4) John Dalton (1808) -- atomic theory, indivisible atoms as building blocks of matter, based on scientific experiments for the first time.
s: At least three correctly ordered points

concepts.name: Thomson's Model and the Gold Foil Experiment
concepts.description: J. J. Thomson's discovery of the electron and his plum-pudding model, and how the Geiger-Marsden gold foil experiment tested and disproved it.
concepts.idea: Thomson found a negatively charged particle inside every atom and pictured it as embedded in a positive sphere; Rutherford's team then fired alpha particles at gold foil to test that picture.
concepts.rule: In 1897, Thomson studied electric current through gases at low pressure and found cathode rays were streams of negatively charged particles (electrons) present in every atom, regardless of the cathode material or the gas used. He proposed the plum pudding model: a sphere of positive charge with electrons distributed through it, like the watermelon analogy (red pulp = positive charge, seeds = electrons). In 1911, Geiger and Marsden, working under Rutherford, aimed alpha particles (positively charged) at thin gold foil. Thomson's model predicted the particles would pass straight through or deflect only slightly, since the positive charge was spread out evenly. Instead, most passed through undeflected, but some were sharply deflected and a few bounced back -- a result Thomson's model could not explain.
concepts.example: Most alpha particles passing straight through the gold foil, with only a few sharply deflected or bounced back, is the key observation that Thomson's evenly-spread-out positive charge could not account for.

questions.q: Explain why Thomson used gas at very low pressure, and different cathode materials, in his cathode ray experiments, based on what this showed about electrons.
questions.a: By varying the gas and the cathode material and still observing the same negatively charged rays, Thomson showed that electrons are not specific to one material or gas but are a fundamental component present in every atom.

questions.q: An alpha particle passes very close to the centre of a gold atom in the gold foil experiment. Using Thomson's model, explain why this should NOT cause a large deflection, and using the actual result, explain why it did.
questions.a: Under Thomson's model the positive charge is spread evenly through the atom, so even a close pass should only cause a small deflection; but the actual result showed a large deflection, because the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus that can exert a much stronger force at close range.

questions.q: Explain, using both Thomson's model and the actual gold foil results, why 'most particles passed through undeflected' does NOT by itself prove the atom has a small nucleus, but 'a few bounced back sharply' does.
questions.a: Both Thomson's model (evenly spread positive charge) and the actual nucleus model would allow most alpha particles to pass through largely undisturbed, since even a concentrated nucleus occupies a tiny fraction of the atom's volume -- so this observation alone is consistent with either model. But sharp deflection and bounce-back require a strong, concentrated force acting over a very short distance, which only a small, dense, highly charged nucleus (not an evenly spread charge) can provide -- so only the second observation rules out Thomson's model.
s: Explains 'mostly undeflected' is consistent with both models

questions.q: A student says, 'Since most alpha particles passed through the foil, the gold foil experiment proved atoms have no positive charge.' Identify the error in this statement.
questions.a: This is incorrect: the gold foil experiment showed that positive charge does exist, but it is concentrated in a tiny nucleus rather than spread throughout the atom; the fact that most particles passed through shows only that most of the atom's volume is empty, not that there is no positive charge.

questions.q: Analyse why Thomson's cathode ray experiment and Rutherford's gold foil experiment are both described as evidence that the atom is NOT indivisible, even though they investigate different things.
questions.a: Thomson's experiment showed that atoms contain smaller negatively charged particles (electrons) that can be detected coming out of them, directly contradicting the idea of the atom as a single indivisible unit. Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed that the atom has internal structure -- a concentrated positive nucleus with mostly empty space around it -- which again means the atom is made of distinguishable parts, not one indivisible whole. Though one experiment is about identifying a particle and the other about how particles are arranged, both show the atom has internal components, disproving Dalton's assumption of indivisibility.
s: Common conclusion: atom is divisible/has structure

questions.q: Was Thomson's plum pudding model a 'failure' as a scientific model, even though it was later disproved? Give a reasoned answer.
questions.a: A reasoned answer either way is acceptable if justified; for example, no, it was not a failure -- it was the first model to correctly show that atoms contain both positive and negative charge, and it made a testable prediction (via the gold foil experiment) that helped scientists learn what was wrong with it and move to a better model, which is how science progresses.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment (different from the gold foil experiment) that could test whether an atom's positive charge is spread out evenly or concentrated in a small region. Describe what result would support each possibility.
questions.a: Example: fire a beam of small positively charged particles at a very thin sheet of a different heavy metal (e.g. platinum) and record where particles land on a surrounding detector screen. If the positive charge is spread out evenly, all particles should pass through with little or no deflection. If the positive charge is concentrated in a small region, most particles should still pass through, but a small number should be deflected at large angles or bounce back, because they passed close to the concentrated charge.
s: Predicted result for evenly spread charge

concepts.name: Rutherford's Nuclear Model, Its Limitations, and the Proton
concepts.description: What Rutherford concluded from the gold foil experiment, why his planetary model could not explain atomic stability, and his discovery of the proton.
concepts.idea: Rutherford placed all of an atom's positive charge and most of its mass in a tiny central nucleus, with electrons orbiting it like planets around the Sun -- but this model could not explain why atoms do not collapse.
concepts.rule: From the gold foil results, Rutherford concluded: most of an atom is empty space; the nucleus is small, dense, and carries all the positive charge and most of the mass; electrons revolve around the nucleus (the planetary model). The nucleus is about 10^5 times smaller than the atom (atom diameter ~ 10^-10 m, nucleus diameter ~ 10^-15 m). Limitation: an orbiting (accelerating) electron should continuously lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, which would make atoms collapse -- but atoms are stable, so the model was incomplete. Rutherford also discovered the proton: the nucleus's positive charge comes from protons, which are much heavier than electrons and carry an equal and opposite charge; since an atom is neutral, its number of protons equals its number of electrons.
concepts.example: If an atom were the size of a 100 m cricket ground, its nucleus would be about the size of a pepper grain at the centre; a helium atom has 2 protons and 2 electrons, a sodium atom has 11 of each.

questions.q: Explain why Rutherford's discovery that atoms are unstable in his own model was actually a useful scientific result, even though it revealed a flaw.
questions.a: It showed exactly what a correct model of the atom needed to explain -- how electrons could move around the nucleus without losing energy and collapsing -- which directed later scientists, such as Bohr, toward the next improved model.
s: Links to guiding the next model

Both I and II

questions.q: Compare what Thomson's and Rutherford's models each say about where the positive charge is located in an atom.
questions.a: Thomson's model placed the positive charge spread evenly throughout the whole sphere of the atom, with electrons embedded in it. Rutherford's model placed all the positive charge concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre, with electrons orbiting around it.

questions.q: Explain the chain of reasoning by which Rutherford's own model created the very problem that Bohr's model later solved.
questions.a: Rutherford's model placed negatively charged electrons in orbit around a positively charged nucleus, similar to planets orbiting the Sun. But according to classical physics, any charged particle moving in a circular path is accelerating, and an accelerating charge should continuously radiate energy. If the electron kept losing energy this way, it would spiral inward and eventually crash into the nucleus, meaning atoms could not exist as stable, lasting structures. Bohr's model solved this by proposing that electrons move only in special 'stationary states' (fixed shells) in which they do not lose energy, directly answering the instability problem created by Rutherford's own planetary picture.
s: Links to what Bohr's model had to solve

questions.q: Rutherford's model was eventually shown to be incomplete. Do you think it should still be considered an important scientific achievement? Justify your answer.
questions.a: A reasoned answer either way is acceptable if justified; for example, yes, because it was the first model to correctly identify that atoms have a small, dense, positively charged nucleus and are mostly empty space -- a conclusion that all later models, including today's, still keep, even though the electron-motion part of the model needed correction.
s: Justification referencing what was kept in later models

questions.q: Design a simple physical model or demonstration (using everyday objects) that could help a younger student understand both the small size of the nucleus compared to the atom, and why Rutherford's electrons-in-orbit idea could not explain atomic stability.
questions.a: Example: use a large empty field (100 m across) with a single pepper grain at the centre to represent the atom and its nucleus, showing how tiny the nucleus is compared to the whole atom. To show the stability problem, spin a ball on a string around a fixed point while slowly loosening your grip on the string -- as the grip loosens ('losing energy'), the ball spirals inward and hits the centre, just as classical physics predicts an orbiting electron should spiral into the nucleus.
s: Both correctly linked to the concepts

concepts.name: Bohr's Model and the Discovery of the Neutron
concepts.description: Bohr's fixed-energy-shell model, which explained atomic stability, and Chadwick's discovery of the neutron, which explained the extra mass of the atom.
concepts.idea: Bohr fixed Rutherford's stability problem by allowing electrons to move only in certain fixed-energy shells; Chadwick later found a third, uncharged subatomic particle that accounts for the rest of an atom's mass.
concepts.rule: In 1913, Bohr proposed that electrons move only in fixed circular paths called shells, orbits, stationary states, or energy levels, named K, L, M, N... (or n = 1, 2, 3, 4...); the K-shell (n=1), closest to the nucleus, has the least energy, and energy increases outward. An electron does not lose energy while moving within one shell; it changes shells only by absorbing or releasing an amount of energy equal to the difference between the two levels. In 1932, James Chadwick discovered the neutron: an uncharged particle with a mass nearly equal to a proton's, found in the nucleus of every atom except hydrogen (protium). This solved the puzzle of why, for example, a helium atom (2 protons) has about four times the mass of a hydrogen atom (1 proton) rather than double: two protons plus two neutrons. Electrons: charge -1, negligible mass; protons: charge +1; neutrons: charge 0, mass roughly equal to a proton's.

concepts.name: Symbols of Elements, Atomic Number, and Mass Number
concepts.description: How elements are given chemical symbols, and the two numbers -- atomic number and mass number -- that describe an atom's nucleus.
concepts.idea: Every element has a one- or two-letter symbol chosen by fixed rules, and every atom of that element has two defining counts: how many protons it has, and how many protons plus neutrons it has.
concepts.rule: Dalton (1803) introduced pictorial element symbols; Berzelius (1813) proposed alphabetic symbols from Latin names; today IUPAC approves all element names and symbols. Rules: the first letter of a symbol is always capital, the second (if any) is always lowercase (H; Al, not AL; Co, not CO); some symbols use a letter other than the second one (Cl for chlorine, Zn for zinc); some come from Latin, Greek or German names (Fe from ferrum/iron, Hg from hydrargyros/mercury, W from wolfram/tungsten). Atomic number (Z) = number of protons in the nucleus = number of electrons in a neutral atom; it identifies the element and its chemical behaviour. Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons (together called nucleons). An atom is written with its mass number above and atomic number below, before the symbol, e.g. mass number 12, atomic number 6, for carbon (C).
concepts.example: Sodium's symbol Na comes from its Latin name natrium; a carbon atom with 6 protons and 6 neutrons has atomic number 6 and mass number 12.

concepts.name: Electronic Configuration and Valency
concepts.description: The Bohr-Bury rules for filling electron shells, and how the electrons in an atom's outermost shell decide its valency.
concepts.idea: Electrons fill shells from the innermost outward, up to a fixed maximum per shell, and an atom's combining capacity depends on how many electrons its outermost shell needs to gain, lose or share to reach a stable octet.
concepts.rule: Bohr-Bury rules: the maximum electrons in a shell is 2n^2 (K=2, L=8, M=18); the outermost shell can hold at most 8 electrons (2 if it is the only shell); shells fill in order, K before L before M, and a shell must be complete before the next one starts filling. The outermost shell with electrons is the valence shell; its electrons are valence electrons. Eight electrons in the outermost shell (2 for helium) is an octet -- a stable, largely unreactive arrangement. An atom with fewer than 4 valence electrons tends to lose them to reach an octet (valency = number of valence electrons); an atom with more than 4 tends to gain electrons to reach an octet (valency = 8 - number of valence electrons); an atom with exactly 4 tends to share electrons. Valency also equals the number of hydrogen or chlorine atoms one atom of the element combines with, e.g. in H2O oxygen's valency is 2, in NH3 nitrogen's valency is 3.
concepts.example: Sodium (2, 8, 1) loses its 1 valence electron, so its valency is 1; oxygen (2, 6) gains 2 electrons to complete its octet, so its valency is 2; carbon (2, 4) shares 4 electrons, so its valency is 4.

questions.q: The chapter states the maximum number of electrons in the outermost shell is 8, but the maximum electrons in the M-shell by the 2n^2 formula is 18. Analyse why these two numbers do not contradict each other, using potassium (atomic number 19, configuration 2, 8, 8, 1) as an example.
questions.a: The 2n^2 formula (giving 18 for the M-shell, n=3) is the absolute maximum a shell can ever hold, but the separate rule that the outermost shell can hold at most 8 electrons applies only while that shell is the outermost one being filled. In potassium, the M-shell is not yet full (only 8 of its possible 18 electrons are filled) because once it reaches 8 electrons -- an octet -- it is treated as 'complete enough' to be outermost, and the next electron starts filling the N-shell instead, giving 2, 8, 8, 1 rather than continuing to fill the M-shell to 18. So the M-shell can hold more electrons later (once it is no longer the outermost shell), but not while it is.

concepts.name: Isotopes, Average Atomic Mass, and Isobars
concepts.description: Atoms of the same element with different neutron counts, how their average mass is calculated, and atoms of different elements that happen to share a mass number.
concepts.idea: Not every atom of an element is identical in mass, because the number of neutrons can vary while the number of protons stays fixed; a fair average mass has to weight each variant by how common it actually is.
concepts.rule: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same atomic number, Z) with different numbers of neutrons and therefore different mass numbers (A). Because isotopes have the same number of electrons (same electronic configuration), they have the same chemical properties but different physical properties (e.g. boiling/melting point). Examples: hydrogen's isotopes protium, deuterium, tritium; carbon's isotopes carbon-12, carbon-13, carbon-14. Named isotope uses in the chapter: uranium-235 as nuclear reactor fuel, cobalt-60 in cancer radiotherapy, iodine-131 for thyroid/goitre treatment, carbon-14 in dating fossils. The weighted average atomic mass of an element = sum of (isotope mass x its fractional abundance) over all its isotopes -- not the simple arithmetic mean, because isotopes do not occur in equal proportions. Isobars are atoms of different elements (different atomic number) that share the same mass number.
concepts.example: Chlorine's weighted average atomic mass = (35 u x 75/100) + (37 u x 25/100) = 35.5 u, not the simple average of 36 u; calcium (Z=20), potassium (Z=19) and argon (Z=18) are isobars because each has mass number 40.

questions.q: Bromine has two isotopes: bromine-79 (50.7% abundance) and bromine-81 (49.3% abundance). Calculate its weighted average atomic mass, and explain in one sentence why this value is close to being exactly halfway between 79 and 81.
questions.a: Weighted average = (79 x 50.7/100) + (81 x 49.3/100) = 40.05 + 39.93 = 79.98 u (approximately 80 u). It is close to exactly halfway (80.0 u) because these two isotopes happen to occur in nearly equal proportion (about 50:50); in general, a weighted average is only close to the simple average when the abundances are close to equal.
s: Correct explanation of why it is close to halfway here

questions.q: A student calculates chlorine's average atomic mass as the simple average of 35 u and 37 u, getting 36 u, instead of the correct weighted average of 35.5 u. Explain the error in the student's method.
questions.a: The student's method assumes both isotopes occur in equal proportion (50:50), but chlorine-35 actually makes up about 75% of atoms and chlorine-37 only about 25%; the correct method must weight each isotope's mass by its actual percentage abundance, not treat them as equally common.

questions.q: Analyse why isotopes and isobars, despite both involving 'same something, different something else', represent fundamentally different relationships between atoms -- one within a single element, and one across different elements.
questions.a: Isotopes share the same atomic number (same element) but differ in mass number, because their neutron count varies while proton count stays fixed -- so they are different versions of one and the same element, with identical chemical behaviour. Isobars share the same mass number but differ in atomic number, meaning their total nucleon count happens to match even though they have different numbers of protons -- so they are entirely different elements with different chemical behaviour, related only by a coincidence of total nucleon count rather than by any true chemical kinship. This is why isotopes are grouped under one element's identity, while isobars are not grouped together at all despite the numerical similarity.
s: States the key conceptual distinction (identity vs numerical coincidence)

questions.q: Given that isotopes of an element behave identically in chemical reactions, do you think it matters which isotope of an element, say carbon, is used in an everyday chemical process (as opposed to a use like carbon dating)? Justify your answer.
questions.a: A reasoned answer either way is acceptable if justified; for example, no, for ordinary chemical processes it usually does not matter which isotope is used, because chemical behaviour depends on the number and arrangement of electrons, which is identical across isotopes -- it only matters for uses (like carbon-14 dating or radiotherapy) that depend on differences in mass or radioactivity between isotopes.
s: Justification distinguishing chemical vs mass/radioactive uses

questions.q: Invent a hypothetical element 'X' with atomic number 30 that has two isotopes of your choosing, and (i) state their mass numbers and neutron counts, (ii) assign a percentage abundance to each (summing to 100%), and (iii) calculate the resulting weighted average atomic mass.
questions.a: Example: element X, atomic number 30, has isotope X-64 (64-30=34 neutrons) at 55% abundance and isotope X-66 (66-30=36 neutrons) at 45% abundance. Weighted average atomic mass = (64 x 0.55) + (66 x 0.45) = 35.2 + 29.7 = 64.9 u.
s: Correct mass numbers/neutron counts for both isotopes
